content: Anemia is a common condition during pregnancy, especially in women from lowand middle-income countries. Traditionally, daily iron supplementation throughout pregnancy has been used to prevent gestational anemia. However, adherence to this regimen is often poor due to side effects, inconsistent supply of supplements, and safety concerns in women with sufficient iron intake. As an alternative, intermittent iron supplementation—administered two or three times a week on non-consecutive days—has been proposed. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of intermittent iron supplementation, either alone or in combination with folic acid or other vitamins and minerals, on pregnancy and neonatal outcomes. The review included 27 trials conducted in 15 countries, though only 21 trials involving 5,490 women contributed data. All studies compared daily iron supplementation with intermittent regimens. The quality of the included studies varied, with many showing high levels of participant dropout. The overall quality of evidence for infant outcomes was rated as low, and for maternal outcomes, very low. Among the 21 trials, three studies examined intermittent iron supplementation alone, 14 studies assessed intermittent iron combined with folic acid, and four studies evaluated intermittent iron combined with multiple vitamins and minerals. These were compared to daily supplementation with the same compositions. For infant outcomes, there was no clear evidence of differences between intermittent and daily regimens in terms of low birthweight (risk ratio [RR] 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.55 to 1.22), mean birthweight (mean difference [MD] 5.13 g; 95% CI -29.46 to 39.72), preterm birth (RR 1.03; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.39), or neonatal death (RR 0.49; 95% CI 0.04 to 5.42). None of the studies reported on congenital anomalies. For maternal outcomes, there was no clear evidence of differences in anemia at term between the two regimens (RR 1.22; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.80). However, women receiving intermittent supplementation experienced fewer side effects (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.37 to 0.84) and were less likely to have high hemoglobin levels (greater than 130 g/L) during the second or third trimester (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.74). There were no significant differences in the risk of iron-deficiency anemia at term (RR 0.71; 95% CI 0.08 to 6.63). No maternal deaths or cases of severe anemia were reported in the studies. Additionally, none of the studies provided data on iron deficiency at term or infections during pregnancy. The majority of the trials (14 out of 21) compared intermittent iron plus folic acid supplementation with daily iron plus folic acid supplementation, involving 4,653 women. The findings for this subgroup were consistent with the overall results. Three studies with 464 women compared intermittent iron alone with daily iron alone, showing no clear differences in mean birthweight, preterm birth, maternal anemia, or maternal side effects. Four studies with 412 women compared intermittent iron plus vitamins and minerals with daily iron plus vitamins and minerals. These studies did not report on infant outcomes but noted fewer maternal side effects in the intermittent group and a higher prevalence of anemia at term. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential differences based on factors such as the timing of supplementation, baseline anemia status, weekly iron dose, and malaria prevalence in the study regions. These variables did not appear to significantly influence the results. In conclusion, this review provides the most comprehensive evidence to date on the effects of intermittent iron supplementation during pregnancy. The findings suggest that intermittent regimens result in similar maternal and infant outcomes compared to daily supplementation but are associated with fewer side effects and a reduced risk of high hemoglobin levels in mid-to-late pregnancy. However, intermittent supplementation may slightly increase the risk of mild anemia near term. While the quality of evidence was low to very low, intermittent iron supplementation may be a viable alternative for pregnant women who are not anemic and have access to adequate antenatal care.
